title: Pagans, Neo-Pagans, Wiccans – Let’s Sort It Out!
summary: Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro voice) survey paganism: what it is, ancient pagan beliefs (animism, shamanism, ancestor worship, earth mother, polytheism, sacrifice, idols and trees), how Christianity suppressed paganism from Constantine onward and demonized pagan gods as Satan, the Renaissance and Enlightenment revival, James Frazer's The Golden Bough and Margaret Murray's witch-cult theories, and modern pagan movements including Wicca (Gerald Gardner, Book of Shadows, Dianic Wicca, Starhawk-era feminist and environmentalist branches, Bowers... Doreen Valiente not named), Heathenry (Asatru and Vanatru), Norwegian black metal church arsons, Druidry, Golden Dawn, and Neopaganism. A listener mail segment closes the episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and definition of paganism
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode on paganism, credit Dave for help, and define paganism as a set of typically nature-based religions that predate the Abrahamic religions.

segments.title: Origin of the word pagan
segments.summary: The word pagan was originally an insult meaning country dweller (paganus) in the Roman Empire for non-Christians, and the hosts discuss how Christianity later used the same playbook against pagans.

segments.title: Ancient versus modern paganism
segments.summary: Modern paganism is described as a new tradition inspired by ancient practices, not an unbroken secret continuation, because few texts survived.

segments.title: Animism, shamanism and ancestor worship
segments.summary: Animism is the belief that objects and nature have spirits that can be influenced through sacrifice and ritual. Shamans enter trance states to communicate with spirits. Ancestor worship is linked to early burial practices with grave goods.

segments.title: Earth Mother and Venus figurines
segments.summary: The earth mother was an early deity, evidenced by Venus figurines about thirty-five thousand years old, and the figure evolved into Gaia in Greek mythology.

segments.title: Polytheism and Mother Nature
segments.summary: Pagan religions are polytheistic, with many gods rather than saints or angels. The hosts speculate that the idea of Mother Nature descends from earlier earth goddesses.

segments.title: Pagan sacrifice and bog bodies
segments.summary: Sacrifice occurred in many ancient religions, with evidence including bog bodies from Germanic and Celtic tribes and the Inca maiden. Claims of widespread baby sacrifice are described as likely exaggerations by enemies, and the hosts discuss the film Apocalypto.

segments.title: Idol worship and tree worship
segments.summary: Idolatry, prohibited in the Ten Commandments, refers to physical representations of gods or spirits, and trees are important in many pagan religions. The hosts summarize the basics of ancient paganism and note that modern pagans draw on archaeology and anthropology.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: The hosts take a break before discussing Christianity's suppression of paganism.

segments.title: Constantine and his successors' laws against paganism
segments.summary: Constantine was the first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity but did not persecute pagans himself. His son Constantius passed the first laws making public paganism illegal, and later Theodosius declared Christianity the state religion and restricted pagan practices, even in homes.

segments.title: Demonization of pagan gods and the origin of Satan
segments.summary: Christianity demonized local pagan gods as the devil. Sir Nunnus, a Celtic antlered god, is discussed as a model for the horned Christian devil, linked to the Greek god Pan. Practicing pagans risked death and persecution, including through the Inquisition.

segments.title: Christian absorption of pagan holidays
segments.summary: The Christian church tweaked pagan holidays like Halloween, Christmas and Easter. Josh notes Easter sunrise services and the pagan goddess Ostara as an example, and Halloween's origins as Samhain.

segments.title: Pagan holidays and Christian propaganda
segments.summary: The hosts describe Christian armies, colonialism and missionaries as means of stamping out paganism, and say Christians used pagan-based holidays. Iin the context of a Stone Mountain sunrise service anecdote.

segments.title: Renaissance and Enlightenment revival of paganism; James Frazer
segments.summary: The Renaissance revived Greek and Roman philosophy and art, and the Romantic poets and Enlightenment thinkers fueled interest in paganism. James Frazer's 1890 book The Golden Bough argued that religions trace to a sacrificed fertility king, and became a handbook for modern pagan movements. Modern historians consider the theory incorrect.

segments.title: Margaret Murray and the unbroken witch cult theory
segments.summary: Egyptologist Margaret Murray argued modern European witches descended from an unbroken fertility cult. The hosts say this has been debunked because Christianity, Judaism and Islam disrupted transmission, though rural folk traditions survive. The Wicker Man and May Pole dancing are mentioned.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: The hosts take a break before moving into modern paganism.

segments.title: Morris dancing and off-topic chat
segments.summary: Josh mentions a friend who is a Morris dancer and not a pagan, noting Morris dances may resemble pagan rites. Chuck and Josh briefly talk about the film Friendship and Tim Robinson.

segments.title: Modern paganism and Norse sources
segments.summary: Modern paganism is its own thing because few ancient texts survived. Norse heathen reconstruction draws on the Eddas and the Viking sagas, which mention pagan practices only incidentally.

segments.title: Golden Dawn and Gerald Gardner's Wicca
segments.summary: The Golden Dawn is described as an early modern pagan-style group practicing magic and Egyptian cult ideas, with Aleister Crowley as a member. Gerald Gardner, a British customs official, claimed in 1939 he was initiated into a witch coven, and his Book of Shadows became central to Wicca.

segments.title: Dianic Wicca, Supreme Court ruling and UK witchcraft laws
segments.summary: Wicca grew in the 1960s and 1970s among feminist and environmentalist groups. Gardnerian and Dianic Wicca are described, with Dianic Wicca founded in 1971 by Susan Budapest and women-only. Debtmer v. Landen (1986) recognized Wicca as religion in US prisons. UK witchcraft laws were repealed in 1951.

segments.title: Heathenry, Asatru, Vanatru and Norwegian black metal church arsons
segments.summary: Heathenry is an umbrella term for Norse and Germanic deity worship, split into Asatru (Aesir, Odin and Thor) and Vanatru (Vanir, nature and prosperity). The hosts discuss the Norwegian black metal scene's shift to heathenry and the church arsons linked to Mayhem members Euronymous and Varg Vikernes.

segments.title: Druidry and modern pagan groups
segments.summary: Modern Druidry is tied to pre-Christian British Isles religion, sees nature as divine, and is often treated as a philosophy. Ross Nichols is named as a founder of modern Druidry, and ceremonial magic is noted as tracing to the Golden Dawn.

segments.title: Neopaganism versus Wicca
segments.summary: Neopaganism is a specific, open, eclectic type of pagan religion that holds all beliefs equal and rejects absolute good and evil. Wicca is more magic-based and esoteric, with initiation and hidden knowledge. The hosts recommend neopaganism.org and advise checking website legitimacy.

segments.title: Listener mail: popcorn cooking tip
segments.summary: Randy with an Eye sends a tip about cooking popcorn in bacon grease in a covered skillet, and says goodbye to the podcast.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank Randy for the tip and invite listeners to send tips to the show's email address; the episode ends with the standard credit.
